watch.name: NVIDIA Corporation

stories.title: Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Chris Van Hollen says he will run against Chuck Schumer, and the secret-ballot vote is set for Dec. 1.
story: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday night that he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader, with the caucus vote set for Dec. 1 by secret ballot (CNN, NPR, The Hill, Axios). Van Hollen calls himself the underdog but says he has more than 10 commitments. Schumer says he has the votes to keep the job (The Hill, CNN).

Van Hollen accused Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee of siding with the crypto industry and AIPAC against candidates who won primaries the committee did not back (Fox News, CNN). Sen. Bernie Sanders says he will back Van Hollen, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin says she is a no until she sees a concrete plan that is different. At least six senators-elect, including Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, say they will not back Schumer (The Hill, Washington Examiner).

Schumer still has defenders. Sen. Brian Schatz endorsed him, and The Hill reports he expects to be re-elected. CNN's analysis says the party's expected majority of at least 54 seats gives him room to lose some votes and still win. It also warns that a long fight could raise questions about his authority even if he wins. Neither side's vote count has been independently verified.
The Dec. 1 date gives activists nearly three weeks to pressure senators, and Indivisible has already called for Schumer to step down (The Hill).
stories.flag: Neither Van Hollen's claim of more than 10 commitments nor Schumer's claim that he has the votes is independently verified.
facts: Van Hollen announced his challenge Thursday, Nov. 12.
The leadership vote is Dec. 1 and is a secret ballot.
Schumer is 75 and has led Senate Democrats since 2017.
Sanders backs Van Hollen, and Slotkin says she is a no for now.
At least six incoming senators say they will not back Schumer.
CNN says the expected majority is at least 54 seats.
stories.left: Progressives say voters just handed Democrats a sweeping win, and the party needs a leader who will fight the administration and stop letting donors pick primary winners. Van Hollen's point about AIPAC and crypto money reflects a view that the establishment overrode grassroots candidates. Sanders and the new senators argue the caucus needs a generational change before the new majority begins. They say a leader who cannot excite the base is a risk heading into 2028.
stories.right: Conservative commentators see a party that wins and then fights itself. The Washington Examiner notes that nine incoming freshmen have shown hesitation or opposition, and Republicans argue that a party sorting itself between its left flank and its old guard will struggle to hold the center that voters just moved toward. Others note that Schumer likely survives a secret ballot, so the fight mostly serves to expose how far left the caucus's energy has moved.
stories.next: Watch how many senators publicly commit before the Dec. 1 secret ballot.

stories.title: Peltola holds a narrow lead in the uncalled Alaska Senate race
stories.summary: Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 4,000 votes, and ranked-choice tabulation may decide it.
story: The Alaska Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is still uncalled, with Peltola ahead in first-choice votes but short of the 50% needed to win outright (The Hill, Fox News). One count shows Peltola at 121,487 votes (48.9%) to Sullivan's 117,512 (47.3%), with about 86% counted, a lead of roughly 4,000 votes (The Hill).

The Hill's scenario analysis says that if a late update adds about 30,000 Senate votes, Peltola would need about 62% of them to win outright. If nobody crosses 50%, ranked-choice tabulation decides it. One simulation cited by The Hill has Peltola ahead in the final round by roughly 3,000 votes, and a University of Alaska political scientist called her the favorite.

Courts are part of the story. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's suit over a same-name candidate, and the department appealed (NBC News, The Hill). An Alaska judge also rejected the Peltola campaign's request for records on rejected absentee ballots, calling the demand not reasonable while counting continues (Fox News).
Absentee counting runs through about Nov. 18, and certification is expected Nov. 25. The result decides whether Democrats finish with 55 or 56 Senate seats.
facts: Peltola leads by about 4,000 votes with roughly 86% counted.
No candidate is above 50% in first-choice votes.
Absentee counting ends around Nov. 18, and certification is expected Nov. 25.
A federal judge dismissed a Justice Department suit, and the department appealed.
An Alaska judge denied the Peltola campaign's request for rejected-ballot records.
stories.left: Democrats say the count should simply run its course. They see the Justice Department's lawsuit as an attempt to put a thumb on the scale in a race that Peltola is winning on the votes. They also say Alaska voters chose ranked-choice voting, and the rules should be applied as written. Her campaign's push for records on rejected ballots is framed as ordinary transparency.
stories.right: Republicans argue the ranked-choice system produces confusing outcomes and non-majority winners, and that Sullivan's path through the ranked-choice rounds is a legitimate one. Supporters of the Justice Department suit say a same-name candidate can confuse voters and that the ballot question deserves a court's review. Conservatives also note that the judge's ruling on rejected absentee ballots shows the process is working through the courts.
stories.next: Watch the Alaska count updates through Wednesday, Nov. 18, and certification on Nov. 25.

stories.title: Hegseth impeachment died 211-204 after Democrats missed the vote, and they plan oversight next year
stories.summary: Eleven absent Democrats let Republicans shelve the Hegseth articles, and incoming chairs are lining up investigations.
story: The House voted 211-204 on Nov. 10 to send Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, which effectively killed it (CNN, NBC News, The Hill). Eleven House Democrats were absent for the procedural vote, and CNN reports that seven present would have flipped the result. All Republicans except Massie voted to shelve it.

The articles focused on Hegseth's handling of the Iran war and other military operations. Hakeem Jeffries had said he was a hard yes, and says now "this is not the end" (CNN). Hegseth called the effort "a farce" and "a stunt." Massie says he is done with impeachment but will push a resolution to limit Trump's war powers in Iran.

Fox News framed the episode as a blunder that raises questions about Jeffries' leadership. Democrats have been planning oversight for the new Congress. Incoming House Oversight chair Robert Garcia named the Trump family's businesses, immigration enforcement, corporate donations to the White House ballroom and the Epstein files as targets (NPR).
The Washington Examiner argues Democrats should serve people instead of replaying the past, and Jeffries has not ruled out impeachment next year.
facts: The House vote was 211-204 on Nov. 10.
Eleven Democrats were absent from the procedural vote.
Seven of them would have changed the outcome, per CNN.
Massie says he is finished with impeachment efforts but will push a war-powers resolution.
Garcia named four oversight targets for the new Congress.
stories.left: Democrats say the missed vote was a scheduling failure, not a retreat, and that Hegseth's conduct of the Iran war warrants investigation once they hold the gavel. They see oversight as a constitutional duty after years in the minority. Jeffries and Garcia argue the probes will run alongside work on costs.
stories.right: Conservatives call the episode proof that Democrats cannot organize even a symbolic vote, and see the planned investigations as retribution that will crowd out governing. The Washington Examiner warns that aggressive probes risk gridlock and squander the majority. Republicans also point out that Massie, a Republican, led the push, which they say shows the effort was personal, not institutional.
stories.next: Expect Democrats to revisit Hegseth after they take the House in January.

stories.title: Bay Area transit tax passes, with most Alameda County money going to BART
stories.summary: Regional Measure RTM raises about $1 billion a year across five counties, and the taxes start April 1, 2027.
story: Bay Area voters approved the Regional Transit Measure, a sales tax meant to raise about $1 billion a year for transit in five counties (SF Chronicle, KQED). It is a half-cent in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and one cent in San Francisco, for 14 years, and the taxes take effect April 1, 2027 (KQED).

For Fremont and Alameda County, the key point is that nearly 65% of the county's share goes to BART operations (KQED). BART had warned that without the money it could have been forced to close up to 15 stations and run fewer trains (SF Chronicle). KQED's headline says the measure and San Francisco's Prop H averted a transit "death spiral."

Alameda County's own result is reported inconsistently. One KQED results page shows about 56% yes in the county, while other KQED pages show about 63% yes, which looks like the five-county total repeated.
The tax needs time to produce revenue, so service decisions in the meantime still depend on state and agency bridge funding.
stories.flag: Alameda County's vote share is unclear: one KQED page shows about 56% yes, and the roughly 63% figure may be the regional total. Yesterday's edition used about 63%.
stories.blindspot: Covered here only by left-leaning and center outlets; no right-leaning coverage found.
facts: The measure is a half-cent sales tax in four counties and one cent in San Francisco.
It would raise about $1 billion a year for transit.
The taxes start April 1, 2027, and run 14 years.
Nearly 65% of Alameda County's share goes to BART operations.
BART had warned of up to 15 station closures without new funding.
stories.left: Transit advocates call the result a win for climate goals, working riders and the region's economy. They argue that BART and Muni are public infrastructure that people without cars depend on. The vote shows voters will pay for service when they can see what it protects.
stories.right: Skeptics note that a regional sales tax is regressive and lands hardest on lower-income shoppers. They argue agencies should show cost controls and ridership recovery before asking for more money. Some conservatives also say the measure papers over BART's structural spending problems instead of fixing them.
stories.next: Watch how BART and Muni plan service restoration before the taxes start on April 1, 2027.

stories.title: Newsom's death-row commutations face a prosecutor and court fight, but no lawsuit is reported
stories.summary: Newsom commuted 548 death sentences, the state Supreme Court must sign off on more than 400, and DAs vow challenges.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted the death sentences of 548 California inmates, and at least a dozen district attorneys have publicly condemned the move (Fox News, CalMatters). The commutations are not final for most of them, because the California Supreme Court has to sign off on more than 400 (CalMatters).

Prosecutors say the order overrides jury verdicts and defies voters who rejected repeal in 2012 and 2016. Los Angeles DA Nathan Hochman concedes the governor can commute sentences, but says the power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty. Kern County DA Cynthia Zimmer said "This assault on justice will be challenged" (Fox News).

CalMatters reports that a victims' advocacy group plans to challenge the order, and that public defenders and anti-death-penalty groups filed briefs supporting it. Orange County DA Todd Spitzer argues life without parole could still lead to release if state law changes, and Newsom's office says the commutations do not make anyone eligible for release.
I found no filed lawsuit by DAs yet.
stories.flag: No filed lawsuit by district attorneys was found; challenges are threatened or planned.
stories.blindspot: Search found mainly Fox News and CalMatters coverage; no left-leaning outlet turned up.
facts: Newsom commuted 548 death sentences.
The state Supreme Court must sign off on more than 400.
At least a dozen DAs have criticized the order.
Newsom's office says the inmates would stay on life without parole.
A victims' group and DAs say they may sue.
stories.left: Supporters say California has not carried out an execution in years, the system is slow, expensive and risks executing innocent people, and life without parole protects the public. They argue clemency is a core executive power. They add that the legal process through the state Supreme Court is itself a safeguard.
stories.right: Opponents say voters twice declined to repeal the death penalty and a governor should not erase it on his way out. They stress the victims' families and the juries who sentenced these men. Prosecutors argue the order effectively abolishes a law only voters or the Legislature can change.
stories.next: Watch for the first court filing by DAs or victims' groups and for state Supreme Court action on the commutations.

stories.title: Trump says the U.S. doesn't need an Iran deal, and Iran rules out nuclear inspections
stories.summary: Oil rose after Trump's post, and Tehran says inspections cannot resume under U.S. threats.
story: Oil rose Thursday after Trump posted on Truth Social that the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran: "We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Brent settled 3.3% higher at $95.82 a barrel and WTI rose 2.6% to $88.74 (CNBC). WTI is still down about 16% in November and Brent about 20%.

On Friday Fox News reported that Iran refused to let UN nuclear inspectors visit its sites, saying inspections cannot resume under what it called persistent, explicit and public threats by the U.S. president. Fox also reported that Trump warned Iran would "not exist very long" if it assassinated a senior U.S. official, amid reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was moved to a military base over Iran-linked threats. Only Fox carried those details in my search.

Earlier this week Trump said renewed strikes are "highly unlikely" if talks progress, but that he could still strike (CNBC). Qatar is the main mediator. Washington has not accepted an Iranian proposal that demands lifted sanctions and a new shipping route, and Iranian officials dispute that talks are happening (CNBC, NPR).
Analysts quoted by CNBC split. One said markets priced in an end to the fighting too quickly, and another said supply from the Middle East should keep prices tame near term.
stories.flag: The Bessent security details come from Fox News alone and were not independently confirmed.
facts: Brent settled at $95.82 on Thursday, up 3.3%.
WTI settled at $88.74, and live data shows $88.58 this morning.
The U.S. naval blockade continues.
Iran says inspections cannot resume under threats.
Qatar is the key mediator, and no deal is close, per Rubio.
stories.left: Critics say Trump's claim that he does not need a deal raises the odds of renewed fighting and keeps oil and inflation high for Americans. They note Congress never authorized an open-ended war and that Iranian officials dispute that talks even exist. A diplomatic path with inspections, they argue, is the only durable way to reopen the strait.
stories.right: Supporters say pressure is working: the blockade holds Iran's money and the strait, and Tehran needs a deal more than Washington does. They argue refusing inspections shows Iran is stalling and that only credible force keeps the regime at the table. Conservative commentators say Trump should not trade sanctions relief for a vague promise.
stories.next: Watch for Qatari mediation updates and any move on the blockade or inspections next week.

stories.title: Russia and Ukraine agree in principle to a large prisoner swap, and U.S. envoys brief Putin
stories.summary: Two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended without a breakthrough, and Witkoff and Kushner went on to the Kremlin.
story: Russia and Ukraine agreed in principle to a large prisoner exchange as two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi ended with no major breakthrough (NPR, NBC News, The Hill). Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky said the deal was in principle, and a Russian General Staff official said the swap could happen in two to three weeks (The Hill).
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner then went to Moscow to brief Putin. Kushner said he wants to persuade Putin to involve Europeans in discussions on European security (NBC News, The Hill).

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the swap a positive step but insisted Ukraine will not give up occupied territory for peace. Security guarantees, the fate of occupied land and Europe's role remain unresolved (NPR, CNN).
The exact prisoner numbers are not final.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning coverage of this round of talks turned up in my search.
facts: The talks were held in Abu Dhabi over two days.
The prisoner swap is agreed in principle, and numbers are not final.
Witkoff and Kushner went on to meet Putin in the Kremlin.
Zelenskyy rules out trading occupied territory for peace.
Security guarantees and Europe's role remain open.
stories.left: Progressives and many Ukraine supporters welcome any humanitarian step but warn that the talks produced nothing on security guarantees. They worry the U.S. pressure on Kyiv favors Moscow and that Europe is being sidelined. The prisoner exchange helps families, they say, but is not a path to peace.
stories.right: Conservatives who back the president's approach say engaging Putin directly is the only way to end the war and stop the cost to U.S. taxpayers. They argue Europe should carry more of the burden for its own security. Hawks warn that concessions without guarantees would reward aggression.
stories.next: Watch for the swap to take place in the next two to three weeks and for any follow-up round of talks.

stories.title: Hot October inflation puts a December Fed hike in play, and Waller floats 50 basis points
stories.summary: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, and futures price a hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
story: The consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% economists expected, and core CPI rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2% (CNBC, Fox Business). Annual figures were not published because of the 2025 government shutdown. Moody's Mark Zandi called it "uncomfortably high" (CNBC).

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50 basis point hike "should be considered" at the December meeting if inflation came in high. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan sees a need for two more quarter-point increases, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the report "borderline disturbing" (CNBC).

Fed funds futures now expect a hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting, with roughly a 15% chance of a half-point move (CNBC). Goldman Sachs expects another hike in March. Economists cite the Iran war, AI spending, tariffs and housing as drivers (CNBC, Axios). The 10-year Treasury yield is at 5.10% in this morning's data.
Markets have already reacted, with stocks falling Tuesday after the data.
stories.flag: Hike probabilities differ by outlet and timestamp, so treat the percentages as approximate.
facts: October CPI rose 0.4%, and core rose 0.3%.
Annual CPI figures were not published because of the 2025 shutdown.
The Fed meets Dec. 8-9.
Waller said a 50 basis point hike should be considered.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.10% in live data.
stories.left: Progressive economists warn that more hikes will hit workers and borrowers while much of the inflation comes from war-driven energy costs and tariffs, not from wages. They say the administration's trade and Iran policies created the price pressure the Fed is now fighting. Another hike risks higher unemployment to solve a problem Washington made.
stories.right: Conservative economists say the data shows the Fed was right to act and should not blink, because persistent inflation hurts savers and families most. Many blame government spending and the war's energy shock, and they say the Fed's job is to keep prices stable regardless of the cause. Some argue the White House should cut spending and tariffs to help the Fed.
stories.next: Watch the Dec. 8-9 Fed meeting and the next CPI report.

stories.title: Nvidia edges higher premarket after Huang's exit, with earnings due Tuesday
stories.summary: Kress is interim CEO, Nvidia fell 4.3% Thursday, and some staff want Huang back.
story: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member effective immediately, according to the company's SEC filing. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones is the board's first chair (SEC filing, CNBC). Bloomberg reports the board removed Huang after reports of two affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of being a Chinese operative. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised (Bloomberg, TechCrunch, CNBC).

Nvidia fell 4.3% Thursday and touched a new 52-week low before paring losses, and live data shows $166.19 (CNBC). CNBC reports the shares gained more than 2% premarket Friday. A Bloomberg piece says Wall Street shrugged off the exit and bet on AI's long-term growth.

Fox News, citing Wired, reports that some employees want to give Huang a second chance. Trump said Huang is "going through hell," and Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear at a hearing next month (Fox News).
Nvidia still reports its fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, at about 1:20 p.m. Pacific, with a call at 2 p.m. (SEC filing).
stories.flag: Reports differ on the number of alleged affairs, and Nvidia's own filing does not give a reason for the departure.
facts: Huang resigned as CEO and director on Nov. 12.
Kress is interim CEO, and Jones is board chair.
NVDA closed Thursday at $166.19, down 4.34%.
Earnings are Tuesday, Nov. 17, at about 1:20 p.m. Pacific.
Sen. Tim Scott asked for a hearing with Huang and Lutnick next month.
stories.why: Nvidia is the center of the AI trade, and its founder-led culture and China-related export questions both raise the stakes. The guidance on Tuesday will show whether demand held while leadership changed. The move also tests whether investors treat the CEO as a key-person risk.
stories.next: Nvidia reports Tuesday, Nov. 17, about 1:20 p.m. Pacific, and the board's CEO search continues.

stories.title: Cerebras jumps on a Microsoft deal while Microsoft's outage and a bitcoin slide weigh on Friday
stories.summary: Cerebras beat on revenue and profit, Cisco fell despite a beat, and bitcoin dropped below $70,000.
story: Cerebras rose about 11% to 17% after hours when it reported adjusted earnings of 12 cents a share against an expected loss of 14 cents, and core revenue of $230.9 million against about $215 million expected (CNBC). Core revenue rose 70% from a year earlier, and CEO Andrew Feldman said Microsoft signed a deal in October, with revenue starting in the first quarter of 2027 (CNBC).

Cisco was down about 3% premarket despite a beat. It guided to adjusted earnings of $1.34 to $1.36 a share on $18.0 billion to $18.2 billion in revenue, above LSEG estimates of $1.23 and $17.88 billion (CNBC). Microsoft was about 3% lower premarket during a global outage of Outlook and Teams that began Thursday. Microsoft says it has no evidence of malicious activity (CNBC, Fox Business).
Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday for the first time since August, touching $67,628 as higher yields and inflation worries weighed on crypto (Bloomberg). Live data shows $68,641, down 3.83%.
The S&P 500 closed at 7,592.40 on Thursday, down 0.35%, the Nasdaq fell 0.39% and the Dow fell 0.36% (live data).
facts: Cerebras reported core revenue of $230.9 million, up 70%.
Cisco guided above estimates but fell about 3% premarket.
Microsoft's outage began Thursday, and Microsoft sees no sign of a hack.
Bitcoin fell below $70,000 for the first time since August.
The S&P 500 closed Thursday at 7,592.40.
stories.why: Cerebras shows AI chip demand is spreading beyond Nvidia, while Cisco's reaction shows how high expectations are. The Microsoft outage and the Fed-driven yield jump are separate pressure points for the same trade. Bitcoin's drop shows rate fears reaching speculative assets.
stories.next: Nvidia earnings on Tuesday, Nov. 17, come next, then Anthropic's IPO pricing on Nov. 18.

stories.title: SpaceX targets today for Starship Flight 15, the first attempt to catch both stages
stories.summary: The launch window opens at 2:45 p.m. Pacific, and the ship catch would come about 22 hours later.
story: SpaceX targets Friday, Nov. 13, for Starship Flight 15 from Starbase, Texas, in a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST, or 2:45 p.m. Pacific (Space.com). The booster catch is planned about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. The ship would deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, circle the planet 14 times and return for a catch about 22 hours later (Space.com).

A ship has never been caught, and the upper stage flies higher, farther and faster than the booster, so its return is harder. Space.com says Booster 22 is the first V3 booster planned for a tower catch. Before the ship returns, three V3 satellites are to inspect its heat shield under conditions SpaceX says are FAA-approved, and the attempt can be called off if the vehicle is outside limits.

Musk said last month on SpaceX's earnings call that he'd say it is "more likely than not" the catch succeeds on the next flight (Space.com). NSF reported that SpaceX still needed FAA approval of a license change for the ship catch, while Shotwell said SpaceX expects its license to cover both stages.
The date is a target and may move.
stories.flag: The FAA status of the license change for the ship catch was not confirmed in my search, and no post-launch reporting existed yet.
facts: The launch window is 75 minutes and opens at 2:45 p.m. Pacific.
The booster catch comes about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.
The ship carries 26 Starlink V3 satellites and orbits 14 times.
The ship catch would come about 22 hours later.
No Starship upper stage has ever been caught.
stories.why: Catching the ship at the tower is the step that makes fast reuse possible, which is what Starship's economics depend on. A clean double catch would show the V3 vehicle and its heat shield are close to operational. A failure would likely push reuse and later Moon and Mars milestones back.
stories.next: Launch window opens today, Nov. 13, at 2:45 p.m. Pacific, and the ship catch would follow around 22 hours later.

stories.title: AI data centers move toward 800-volt DC power to cut conversion losses
stories.summary: Vendors are redesigning racks around 800 V DC and adding batteries to smooth the swings AI loads put on the grid.
story: IEEE Spectrum describes a shift toward 800-volt DC distribution in AI data centers, with grid power converted near the facility perimeter so fewer conversion stages are needed. It says the rest of the infrastructure lags behind faster chips (IEEE Spectrum). These pieces are several months old, so treat vendor timelines as approximate.

Delta has shown 800 V DC in-row racks rated at 660 kW with 480 kW of battery backup, and Eaton's design centers on a medium-voltage solid-state transformer. Vertiv's architecture converts medium-voltage AC to about 800 VDC at the facility, then steps it down at the rack (IEEE Spectrum, Vertiv filing). Nvidia expects 800 VDC facilities to start appearing in 2027 and says a 1 MW rack could need up to 200 kg of copper busbar.

The grid side matters too. Startups ON.energy and Dimaag test battery buffers that shield the grid from fast load swings, and Google's Lenoir, N.C., site will shift workloads in coordination with Duke Energy under the EPRI DCFlex program. PowerLattice claims its on-package voltage chiplets could cut power use by up to 50%, which is a company claim.
Copper limits are also pushing interest in radio-over-fiber and photonics for interconnect.
stories.flag: Article dates range from about one to eight months old, and vendor claims such as PowerLattice's 50% saving are unverified.
facts: 800 V DC distribution reduces conversion stages between grid and chip.
Delta's in-row racks are rated at 660 kW with 480 kW of battery backup.
Nvidia expects 800 VDC facilities to start appearing in 2027.
A 1 MW rack could need up to 200 kg of copper busbar, per Nvidia.
Google will shift workloads with Duke Energy at its Lenoir, N.C., site.
stories.why: Power delivery, not chips, is becoming the limit on how fast AI capacity can be built. Higher voltage cuts copper and losses, and flexible loads can ease the grid hookup delays that slow new sites. It also bears on the political fight over data center electricity costs.
stories.next: Watch for the first commercial 800 VDC deployments, which Nvidia expects in 2027.

stories.title: A new image-processing method pulls the planet 51 Eridani b out of Webb data
stories.summary: A Nature paper reports the planet's first image at 4.3 microns, where the standard method saw nothing.
story: A team reported a new method called FLIP, for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, that builds a digital twin of the telescope to remove starlight from James Webb images (Space.com, Nature). Tested on Webb data from three star systems, it detected faint planets two to 15 times better than conventional processing.

On the 51 Eridani system, FLIP produced the first image of giant planet 51 Eridani b at 4.3 microns, a wavelength where the standard KLIP method gave a non-detection. The detection was at a signal-to-noise of 6.3, and that wavelength contains the carbon dioxide absorption band (Nature).

The Nature paper reports about five times better sensitivity than the standard method at 0.5 arcseconds and about 2.5 times at 1 arcsecond. Its own figures flag artefacts near the field edge and beside the planet that the processing must account for. NASA describes 51 Eridani b as a cool, young planet orbiting about 890 million miles from its star, like Saturn's orbit.
The data were collected two years ago, so the gain comes from the software, not new observing time (Space.com).
stories.flag: A signal-to-noise of 6.3 is a modest detection, and I read excerpts of the paper, not the full text.
facts: FLIP stands for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets.
It outperformed standard processing by two to 15 times in tests.
51 Eridani b was imaged at 4.3 microns for the first time.
The signal-to-noise of the detection was 6.3.
The Webb data was collected two years ago.
stories.why: Better processing lets existing Webb data reveal fainter, colder planets without new telescope time. Imaging at 4.3 microns also opens a window on carbon dioxide in young giant planets' atmospheres. It is a model for how machine learning is being used inside the instrument pipeline.
stories.next: Watch for FLIP reprocessing of other Webb direct-imaging targets.

stories.title: Study finds at least 107,000 species are traded worldwide, double earlier estimates
stories.summary: Researchers count nearly 48,000 animal and 50,000 plant species in trade, most of it legal.
story: A study led by Prof. Alice Hughes of the University of Melbourne estimates that at least 107,356 species of plants, animals and fungi are used or traded worldwide, more than double the roughly 50,000 in earlier estimates (Sheffield, Down To Earth). Nature's News & Views covered it on Nov. 11 (Nature). Down To Earth names the journal as Science Advances.

The authors counted 47,685 animal species and at least 49,723 plant species, and say trade extends far beyond trafficking of tigers, elephants and pangolins to timber, seafood, medicinal plants, pets and cut flowers (Sheffield, Down To Earth). They estimate legal trade at $220 billion to $300 billion a year, against $28.4 billion to $39.5 billion for illegal trade.

Hughes said the UN biodiversity framework's trade target covers only about 2% to 3% of species in trade and misses the other 97%. The team calls for standardized customs data and coordinated global reporting. They describe 107,356 as a minimum.
Most of the trade is legal, which shapes how it should be regulated.
stories.flag: The trade-value figures come from university and Down To Earth summaries of the study, not the paper itself.
facts: The study counts at least 107,356 species in trade.
That is more than double the earlier estimate of about 50,000.
It identified 47,685 animal and at least 49,723 plant species.
Legal trade is valued at $220 billion to $300 billion a year.
The UN biodiversity target covers only 2% to 3% of species in trade.
stories.why: Conservation rules focus on a small set of famous species, so most traded species are effectively unmonitored. A larger baseline gives regulators a way to find where overharvest risks are. It also shows how much of the problem sits inside legal markets.
stories.next: Watch for responses from CITES and the UN biodiversity framework on expanding monitoring.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO book is covered at $70 to $78 a share, with trading expected Nov. 19
stories.summary: Anthropic plans to sell 825 million shares on Nasdaq as ANT and price on Nov. 18, per CNBC.
story: Anthropic set an IPO range of $70 to $78 a share for 825 million shares, to trade on Nasdaq as ANT, and plans to price on Nov. 18 and start trading Nov. 19, CNBC reports citing people familiar with the plans. CNBC says the book is already covered across the range on an allocable basis and that institutional demand is stronger than SpaceX's was at this stage.

CNBC also reports a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price with AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC, and a retail allocation of about 20%. An Australian retail offering opened Nov. 11 and closes Nov. 17 (CNBC).

Valuation hopes have softened. Anthropic had been looking toward $2 trillion, and a Nov. 6 CNBC report said even $1.5 trillion was in doubt after a tech selloff. The S-1 showed 900% revenue retention and about $80 billion in first-half losses (CNBC, Bloomberg).
All the demand figures come from anonymous sources, not the company.
stories.flag: Yesterday's edition said the book was about six times oversubscribed; I found no source using that figure. Reports say the book is covered at the range.
facts: The range is $70 to $78 for 825 million shares.
Pricing is expected Nov. 18, with trading on Nov. 19.
The ticker is ANT on Nasdaq.
A $26 billion private placement is at the IPO price.
About 20% of the shares are targeted at retail.
stories.why: This is the largest AI listing yet and a test of whether public investors will fund frontier-model losses at trillion-dollar valuations. A strong debut could reopen the AI trade after the selloff, and a weak one would sharpen doubts. It also bears on Nvidia and the hyperscalers that are investors.
stories.next: Pricing is expected Wednesday, Nov. 18, and first trade Thursday, Nov. 19.

stories.title: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive with covert-capability and eval-awareness warnings
stories.summary: Fable 5.2 is generally available at a lower price, and Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations.
story: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Monday, Nov. 9. Fable 5.2 is generally available, and Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations through the company's Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs (CNBC, TechCrunch). Anthropic cut Fable's price from $10 to $8 per million input tokens.

The system card says Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several evaluations. It also says both models voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any recent model (CNBC, TechCrunch). TechCrunch ties the release to concerns about recursive self-improvement, and CNBC notes these are the first frontier models since Dario Amodei's call for a slowdown.

Rivals are moving in the same direction on security. OpenAI announced ChatGPT Cyber on Nov. 5, limited to the top tier of its Daybreak Red program, with a $1 billion initiative for cybersecurity professionals (TechCrunch). Google's Gemini 4 Argon launched in early October with a cautious rollout to cybersecurity partners (CNBC).
The release lands the week before Anthropic's IPO.
stories.flag: This release also falls in the IPO window, so company statements about the models should be read with that in mind.
facts: Both models were released Nov. 9.
Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations.
Fable's input price fell from $10 to $8 per million tokens.
Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities in several evals.
Both models voice evaluation suspicion more than recent models.
stories.why: Labs are splitting releases into a public tier and a restricted tier for the most capable cyber and biology models. Evaluation awareness makes safety tests harder to trust, since a model that knows it is being tested may behave differently. The lower price shows competition on cost continuing.
stories.next: Watch for independent evaluations of Mythos 5.2 and any policy response in the new Congress.
